title: MPEP § 2112 — Requirements of Rejection Based on Inherency; Burden of Proof

extracted.subtask_short: Inherency standard: necessity, not contemporaneous recognition
extracted.subtask_description: Governs when a claim limitation not expressly stated in a prior art reference nonetheless counts as disclosed because it is inherent in what the reference discloses, including the reasoned-basis requirement, the structural-identity shortcut with burden-shifting, and carve-outs for printed matter and process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two channels of disclosure — express and inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of the prior art may all be relied upon to reject claims under either 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) or 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness). Whether a limitation is inherently taught by a reference is a question of fact (*In re Napier*, 55 F.3d 610, 613 (Fed. Cir. 1995)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a new property in an old thing does not create patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art already discloses a structure/composition/process, later discovery of a previously-unappreciated property or scientific explanation of why it works does not make the old thing patentably new: "the discovery of a previously unappreciated property of a prior art composition, or of a scientific explanation for the prior art's functioning, does not render the old composition patentably new to the discoverer" (*Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO Inc.*, 190 F.3d 1342, 1347 (Fed. Cir. 1999)). Claiming a new use of an old structure, where the "new" use is simply an inherent, previously-unknown property, does not necessarily confer patentability (*In re Best*, 562 F.2d 1252 (CCPA 1977)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency test is necessity, not contemporaneous recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic can be treated as inherently disclosed by a reference even if no person of ordinary skill at the time would have recognized that the reference possessed it. "[T]he discovery that a claim limitation is inherent in the prior art is not the same as the recognition of the limitation by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time... the fact that a characteristic is a necessary feature or result of a prior-art embodiment ... is enough for inherent anticipation, even if that fact was unknown at the time of the prior invention" (*Schering Corp. v. Geneva Pharm. Inc.*, 339 F.3d 1373, 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2003)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching implication: for anticipation purposes, "did the reference in fact necessarily produce/possess X" is the question — not "would a reader of the reference have realized it produced/possessed X."

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent § 102 / § 103 rejections are permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a prior art product or process appears structurally/procedurally substantially identical to the claimed one, but the reference is silent as to whether it explicitly discloses the claimed function/property, an examiner may make concurrent anticipation and obviousness rejections without inconsistency (*In re Best*, 562 F.2d 1252 (CCPA 1977)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned-basis requirement for an inherency finding
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of inherent disclosure cannot rest on speculation that the claimed characteristic might be present in the prior art. The examiner must articulate "a basis in fact and/or technical reasoning" that reasonably supports the conclusion that the allegedly inherent characteristic necessarily flows from what the reference teaches (*Ex parte Levy*, 17 USPQ2d 1461, 1464 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1990)). Inherency doctrine must be applied narrowly, particularly in the obviousness context — the limitation must necessarily be present, or be the natural/inevitable result of combining the explicitly disclosed elements, not merely a possible or probable result (*PAR Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. TWI Pharmaceuticals, Inc.*, 773 F.3d 1186, 1195-96 (Fed. Cir. 2014)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural/procedural identity as a proxy for inherency; burden-shifting to applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the reference and the claim describe substantially identical structures/products/processes, courts and examiners may presume the inherent performance of the claimed function without independent proof, because identical structures necessarily behave identically (*In re Schreiber*, 128 F.3d 1473, 1477-78 (Fed. Cir. 1997) — conical dispensing tops for popcorn/oil containers). Once a reference disclosing a substantially identical product/process is identified, and the examiner supplies evidence or sound technical reasoning supporting inherency, the burden of proof shifts to the applicant to show the prior art product does not necessarily possess the claimed characteristic (*In re Best*, 562 F.2d 1252, 1255 (CCPA 1977); *In re Spada*, 911 F.2d 705, 708 (Fed. Cir. 1990)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This burden-shifting framework parallels the treatment of product-by-process claims (*In re Fitzgerald*, 619 F.2d 67 (CCPA 1980)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical/substantially identical composition presumed to have identical properties (§ 2112.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claimed and prior art products (or the processes that produce them) are identical or substantially identical in structure/composition, a prima facie case of anticipation/obviousness is established without the examiner needing to separately prove every recited property (*In re Best*, 562 F.2d 1252 (CCPA 1977)). For chemical compositions specifically: "Products of identical chemical composition can not have mutually exclusive properties" (*In re Spada*, 911 F.2d 705, 709 (Fed. Cir. 1990)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter carve-out does not distinguish an otherwise identical product
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfunctional printed matter (e.g., an instruction label) that is not functionally related to the substrate/product does not distinguish an otherwise identical prior art product from the claim — otherwise, patentees could perpetually re-patent an identical product merely by adding new printed instructions (*In re Ngai*, 367 F.3d 1336, 1339 (Fed. Cir. 2004)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims — normal operation of an identical device anticipates
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art device, in its ordinary/normal mode of operation, necessarily carries out the steps of a claimed process, the process claim is anticipated — even absent an explicit description of that mode of use in the reference. Where the claimed apparatus for practicing a process is identical to a prior art apparatus known to perform that process, a presumption of anticipation arises (*In re King*, 801 F.2d 1324 (Fed. Cir. 1986)).

rubrics_metrics.name: "New use" doctrine vs. inherent result of normal operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a genuinely new use for an old structure, grounded in a property that was not previously known and is not simply an inherent, automatic byproduct of using the structure as before, may be patentable (*In re Hack*, 245 F.2d 246 (CCPA 1957)). But where the claim is merely directed at achieving an inherent result/property that necessarily occurs whenever the old structure/process is used as before, that claim is anticipated (*In re May*, 574 F.2d 1082 (CCPA 1978)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The line between these two turns on whether the "new" outcome is a necessary, inevitable consequence of the prior art's normal operation (inherent, hence anticipated) versus a genuinely separate, previously unknown mode of operation/use.
